query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small interstitial carbon addition to a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., Nb-Mo-Ta-W) and applying an aging treatment will form a stable dispersion of nanoscale (Ta,Nb)C carbides that increases high-temperature strength and creep resistance while acting as sinks for irradiation-induced defects, thereby maintaining or improving irradiation stability relative to the undoped baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Nb-Mo-Ta-W refractory high-entropy alloy, single-phase BCC, homogenized and recrystallized to a coarse or intermediate grain size without secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Add 0.3–1.0 at.% carbon to the alloy and perform a controlled aging treatment (post-solution anneal) to precipitate nanoscale (Ta,Nb)C carbides within grains and at non-continuous grain-boundary sites.
generation.conditions: Thermomechanical processing: solutionize at 1300–1400 °C followed by aging at 1000–1200 °C to nucleate carbides; mechanical testing at 900–1200 °C; irradiation exposure at 400–800 °C to representative ion (e.g., Fe) or neutron doses in the low-to-moderate dpa regime typical of screening tests.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, high number density of nanoscale (Ta,Nb)C precipitates (coherent or semi-coherent with the BCC matrix) that remain finely dispersed under test temperatures and irradiation; absence of continuous carbide films at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via Orowan bypass and reduced dislocation climb at high temperature; enhanced grain-boundary cohesion and pinning that reduces grain-boundary sliding; and increased sink strength for point defects and dislocation loops under irradiation, promoting recombination and lowering defect accumulation. The high-entropy matrix’s sluggish diffusion complements carbide stability, limiting coarsening and preserving sink density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the carbon-free baseline, the carbon-doped and aged alloy will exhibit higher yield/flow strength and reduced creep rate at 900–1200 °C, and under irradiation will show lower irradiation-induced hardening and defect/void density. The direction of improvement is expected to be positive; the precise magnitude is uncertain without direct evidence here but should be measurable beyond experimental uncertainty.
generation.baseline: The same Nb-Mo-Ta-W alloy without carbon addition, processed identically (solutionize and hold without aging-induced carbides), single-phase BCC, similar grain size.
generation.boundary: Effects are expected for single-phase BCC Nb-Mo-Ta-W-like RHEAs with low carbon additions that avoid continuous grain-boundary carbide films; aging must produce intragranular nanoscale carbides rather than coarse or networked precipitates. Excess carbon or inappropriate thermal schedules that drive coarsening or continuous boundary films may cause embrittlement and negate benefits. Very high temperatures (>~1200 °C) or very high irradiation doses may destabilize precipitates and reduce benefits.
generation.uncertainty: No temporally eligible prior evidence is provided here to quantify the size of strength/creep improvements or exact irradiation stability; precipitate coherency, distribution control, and long-term coarsening behavior in this specific alloy system are uncertain. There is also uncertainty about the balance between intragranular and grain-boundary carbide formation and its impact on ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloys: (1) baseline Nb-Mo-Ta-W (equiatomic) and (2) the same composition with 0.5 at.% C. Solutionize both at 1350 °C, then age only the C-doped alloy at 1100 °C to precipitate carbides. Confirm microstructures by TEM/APT. Conduct high-temperature tensile tests at 900, 1000, and 1200 °C and constant-load creep tests at a fixed stress. Irradiate both alloys at 600 °C to a moderate dpa using heavy ions (e.g., Fe) and characterize nanoindentation hardness changes, defect loop/void densities by TEM, and precipitate stability (size/number density) pre- and post-irradiation.
measurements: Creep rate or time-to-rupture under constant load at 1000–1100 °C
Defect loop and void density by TEM after irradiation
Precipitate size and number density (TEM/APT) before/after irradiation
Grain-boundary carbide continuity (EBSD/TEM) and ductility metrics (elongation to failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the C-doped, aged alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature strength and a decrease in creep rate relative to the baseline, or if irradiation leads to equal or greater hardening, defect/void densities, or significant precipitate dissolution/coarsening compared to the baseline; additionally, formation of continuous grain-boundary carbides causing reduced ductility relative to baseline would falsify the claim of maintained mechanical performance.
